learn.hook: A play is a story that comes alive — actors become the characters right in front of you!
points: 'Say the Right Thing' is a funny play about manners and choosing our words. Here is our own short scene.
A play is a story written to be acted on stage; it is told mostly through dialogue (what the characters say).
The speaker's name comes before each line, and the cast is the list of characters.
Stage directions, usually in brackets or italics, tell actors how to move or speak. They are not spoken aloud.
Plays are divided into acts and scenes. The people who watch are the audience.

example.q: Read: (A busy kitchen. AMMA is rolling rotis. TINU runs in.) TINU: Amma, give me water! AMMA: (raising an eyebrow) Is that how we ask? TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water? AMMA: Of course, beta. (She hands him a glass.) Which parts are stage directions, and how is Tinu's second line different from his first?
steps: Words in brackets, like '(raising an eyebrow)', are stage directions.
First line: an order — 'give me water!'
Second line: a polite request with 'may I' and 'please'.
example.answer: The bracketed parts are stage directions; Tinu's second line is polite because he uses 'May I please…'.

learn.reallife: School annual-day plays, Ramlila performances and street plays (nukkad natak) all use dialogue and stage directions.

games.title: Play facts
items: Stage directions are read aloud by the actors.
They guide the actors and are not spoken.
A play is told mostly through dialogue.
Characters tell the story by speaking.
A play can be divided into acts and scenes.
Acts are big parts; scenes are smaller parts.
The audience is the group of people who watch a play.
They watch and enjoy the performance.
The cast is the list of characters in a play.
It is usually given at the beginning.

quiz.q: In a play, words in brackets like '(raising an eyebrow)' are called:
quiz.explain: They tell the actor what to do — they are stage directions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks everything in a play is dialogue

quiz.q: Do actors speak the stage directions aloud?
options: Yes, but only at the end
Only the audience reads them aloud
No, stage directions only guide the actors
quiz.explain: Stage directions are instructions for actions and tone; they are not spoken.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every written word in a play is spoken

quiz.q: 'TINU: Amma, give me water!' 'AMMA: Is that how we ask?' Why does Amma say this?
quiz.explain: 'Give me water!' sounds like an order; Amma reminds him to ask nicely.
quiz.mistake: Misses the hint in Amma's question

quiz.q: The conversation between characters in a play is called:
quiz.explain: Dialogue is the talk between characters.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up words from poems and books

quiz.q: The list of all the characters in a play is called the:
quiz.explain: The cast lists the characters (and sometimes the actors who play them).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the cast with the people watching or the place

quiz.q: Plays are usually divided into:
quiz.explain: Acts are the big sections of a play; scenes are smaller parts inside them.
quiz.mistake: Uses the parts of a poem or book

quiz.q: 'TINU: (smiling) Amma, may I please have some water?' Which polite words does Tinu use?
quiz.explain: He asks with 'may I' and adds 'please' — a polite request.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the actual words in the line

quiz.q: The people who watch a play are called the:
quiz.explain: The audience watches; the cast acts; the director guides the actors.
quiz.mistake: Confuses people who watch with people who perform

teach.ask: Gappu wants to act in the school play. How is a play written differently from a story?
teach.praise: Yay! I'll read my lines and follow the stage directions in brackets!
teach.nudge: What do the words in brackets tell the actors?

learn.hook: The same request can sound like a command or a kind question — it all depends on the words you choose!
points: Please, thank you, sorry and excuse me are polite words that make conversations kind.
Polite requests often begin with 'Could you…?', 'Would you…?' or 'May I…?'
'May I' asks for permission. 'Can' usually shows ability: 'Rani can swim.'
When someone thanks you, reply 'You're welcome.'
Our tone of voice and body language also show respect.

example.q: Make this polite: 'Give me your pencil.'
steps: Begin with a polite modal: 'Could you…'
example.answer: Could you please lend me your pencil?

learn.reallife: At home, in shops, on the bus and in class, polite words make people happy to help you.

games.title: Say the right thing
pairs: You step on a friend's foot.
You need to pass through a crowd.
You want to borrow a book.
Could I borrow your book, please?

items.text: Rahul is very strong; he ___ lift this heavy box.

quiz.q: What is the most polite way to ask for the salt at dinner?
options: Could you please pass the salt?
quiz.explain: 'Could you please…' is a gentle, polite request.
quiz.mistake: Thinks short commands are fine at the table

quiz.q: If you bump into someone by mistake, you should say:
quiz.explain: We say sorry when we have hurt or troubled someone, even by mistake.
quiz.mistake: Uses a polite word in the wrong situation

quiz.q: How should you ask to enter the staff room?
quiz.explain: 'May I…?' asks for permission politely.
quiz.mistake: Announces instead of asking permission

quiz.q: When someone says 'Thank you' to you, the best reply is:
quiz.explain: 'You're welcome' is the polite answer to thanks.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up polite phrases

quiz.q: Which phrase do we use to get someone's attention politely?
quiz.explain: 'Excuse me' is polite; the others can sound rude.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any attention-getting word is polite

quiz.q: In 'May I go out, sir?', the word 'may' shows:
quiz.explain: Here 'may' is used to ask permission.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'may' (permission) with 'can' (ability)

quiz.q: In 'Rani can swim very well', the word 'can' shows:
quiz.explain: 'Can' here tells us what Rani is able to do.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'can' always asks for permission

quiz.q: Which sentence is a polite request?
options: Would you help me carry these books, please?
quiz.explain: 'Would you… please?' turns an order into a polite request.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a command with a request

teach.ask: Gappu shouted 'Give me grains!' at the farmer. How should he say it politely?
teach.praise: 'Could you please give me some grains? Thank you!' — the farmer smiled at me!
teach.nudge: Which magic word did you forget? And how can Gappu begin the request?

learn.hook: If your teacher says 'Hold your horses!', don't look for horses in the classroom!
points: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
'It's raining cats and dogs' means it is raining heavily — no animals fall from the sky!
Taking an idiom literally (word for word) can cause funny misunderstandings — a common source of humour in plays.
Good communication means choosing words that the listener will understand.
Tone matters: the same words can sound kind or rude depending on how we say them.

example.q: Dadi says, 'Hold your horses!' and Chintu looks around for horses. Why is this funny, and what did Dadi mean?
example.answer: It's funny because Chintu takes the idiom literally; Dadi meant 'Wait, be patient.'

learn.reallife: Cricket commentators, film dialogues and grandparents all love idioms — knowing them helps you understand people better.

games.title: Idiom meanings
pairs: cost an arm and a leg

items.text: Seema was ___ when she won the prize.
Riya felt ___, so she stayed home from school.
The test was ___ — I finished it in ten minutes!
Don't ___ — the party is a surprise!
items.answer: let the cat out of the bag
options: let the cat out of the bag

quiz.q: What does 'a piece of cake' mean?
quiz.explain: 'The quiz was a piece of cake' means it was very easy.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What does 'break the ice' mean?
options: start a friendly conversation when people feel shy
quiz.explain: People 'break the ice' at a new class or party by talking first.
quiz.mistake: Reads the words literally

quiz.q: What does 'once in a blue moon' mean?
quiz.explain: Something that happens once in a blue moon happens hardly ever.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about the real moon

quiz.q: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
quiz.explain: It means to reveal a secret, often by accident.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: What does 'hold your horses' mean?
quiz.explain: It asks someone to slow down and wait.
quiz.mistake: Pictures real horses

quiz.q: What does 'under the weather' mean?
quiz.explain: 'I'm under the weather' means 'I'm not feeling well.'
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about the weather

quiz.q: Teacher: 'Use your head!' Golu taps his head on the desk. Why is this funny?
options: The teacher asked him to dance
Golu took the idiom literally; it means 'think carefully'
quiz.explain: 'Use your head' means think. Golu's literal action creates a funny misunderstanding.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that the joke is about an idiom

quiz.q: What does 'over the moon' mean?
quiz.explain: If you are over the moon, you are delighted.
quiz.mistake: Imagines a real trip to the moon

teach.ask: Gappu's friend said 'Break a leg!' before his show, and Gappu got scared. Explain idioms to him.
teach.praise: Phew! 'Break a leg' means 'good luck'! Idioms are tricky but fun!
teach.nudge: Does an idiom mean exactly what its words say?
